title: Mannheim water capacity constraint response and staffing
subtitle: Also covered: police budget vote opinion, transit hub public art, road safety funding, and deferred motions.
overview: Council spent most of the night on the water capacity constraint in the Mannheim Service Area. Staff presented a preliminary list of short, medium and long-term projects. Council approved new permanent and temporary water positions {{vote:m9}}. It asked for a plain-language report on the situation for stakeholders and the public {{vote:m10}}. Staff will also hold an industry workshop before February 27 {{vote:m17}} and give bi-monthly supply and demand updates {{vote:m18}}. A risk-management report on development is due in March {{vote:m15}}.

A proposal to keep approving servicing agreements using up to half of planned new capacity was referred to the February 10 Sustainability, Infrastructure, and Development committee {{vote:m14}}. Staff said they cannot sign off on new approvals while the system operates above sustainable capacity. For residents, this means new approvals in the Mannheim area remain on hold for now, while existing permits continue.

Council also approved a public art expenditure for the Kitchener Central Transit Hub and consultations on a regional arts council {{vote:m7}}. It heard a legal opinion that the December 16 police budget vote procedure was incorrect, and approved those minutes {{vote:m3}}. Council also asked staff to report on funding school-zone road safety {{vote:m21}}.

decisions.detail: Council approved up to nine full-time-equivalent positions to address the Mannheim water capacity constraint, with 2026 costs of about $1.2 million from the Water Stabilization Reserve.

Staff are to prepare an in-depth report from publicly available information describing the Mannheim constraint and the path to address it, and make it available to stakeholders, consultants and the public.
Staff will report back in March 2026 with a risk-management approach to development, breaking down existing and planned water capacity for 2026, 2027, 2028 and beyond.

Staff will convene a workshop with development professionals before February 27, 2026 on immediate, medium and long-term solutions, including a transition plan toward 20% operational resiliency, and report in March.
Staff are directed to give Council bi-monthly updates on year-over-year available water supply and demand capacities.

decisions.item: Transit hub art and arts council
decisions.detail: Council approved up to $600,000 from the Public Art Reserve for the Kitchener Central Transit Hub, an accounts write-off, and consultation on a Waterloo Region Arts Council with a report by August 2026.
Staff will report by Q2 2026 on allocating the remaining Road Safety Reserve to school-zone safety and on future funding options, after the automated speed enforcement wind-down.
Council approved the minutes of the December 16, 2025 special meeting after defeating an amendment to include a transcript of the related item.

debate: Industry delegates argued the issue is risk management rather than supply, and that a development pause threatens jobs, financing and municipal revenues. They said their own analysis shows enough capacity. A councillor noted that analysis was prepared by industry members rather than water engineers and should be cross-checked with staff.

Staff said they cannot sign off on new servicing approvals while wells run above sustainable capacity, citing safe drinking water duties and liability. Proponents of the 50% allocation motion said council makes the policy call and that approvals would still need professional sign-off.

Several councillors questioned using consultants instead of permanent hires. Staff replied that consultants are scarce and not available for multi-year projects, and that recruitment would proceed alongside interim consultants.

Delegates opposed to the Wilmot land assembly argued that water uncertainty justifies cancelling it. Staff said the proposed reallocation from Wilmot wells still leaves enough water for Wilmot through 2051.

On the December 16 minutes, one councillor said voting against would signal displeasure, while others said minutes should record what happened. A transcript amendment was defeated because it would add burden and the legal opinion already clarified the matter.
